RULE AGAINST PERPETUITIES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Jordan T. Reyes is reviewing this information sheet in connection with The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust, created by Jordan Alex Lee as settlor, naming Jordan Alex Lee as trustee. This information sheet describes, on a general informational basis only, California's statutory Rule Against Perpetuities, Probate Code §§ 21200–21231 (the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities as adopted and modified in California), which limits how long a nonvested property interest or an unexercised power of appointment created under an instrument such as The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust may remain contingent before it must vest, terminate, or otherwise resolve. It describes the statutory two-alternative validity test, the parallel rule for powers of appointment, the judicial reformation remedy available for an interest that would otherwise violate the rule, and certain exclusions the statute itself states. This information sheet does not identify, evaluate, or reach any conclusion about whether any specific provision of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust, or of any other instrument, actually satisfies or violates this rule; whether a particular nonvested property interest or power of appointment is valid under Probate Code §§ 21200–21231 depends on the precise terms of the instrument creating it and is a legal determination this information sheet does not make.

STATUTORY CITATION, SUPERSESSION OF THE COMMON LAW RULE, AND SCOPE
The statutory scheme now governing how long a nonvested property interest — a property interest that has not yet vested, such as many contingent trust interests — and an unexercised power of appointment may remain contingent in California is Probate Code Part 2 (§§ 21200–21231), formally cited as the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities. This statutory scheme supersedes California's earlier common-law rule against perpetuities (the traditional rule requiring that an interest be certain to vest, if at all, within "lives in being plus 21 years") rather than operating alongside it. Except for a property interest or power of appointment whose validity has already been determined in a judicial proceeding or by a settlement among interested persons, the statutory scheme applies to nonvested property interests and unexercised powers of appointment regardless of whether they were created before, on, or after January 1, 1992.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21200 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the statutory title of Part 2, Chapter 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21200.)
  "This chapter supersedes the common law rule against perpetuities."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21201 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, supersession of the common law rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21201.)
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), this part applies to nonvested property interests and unexercised powers of appointment regardless of whether they were created before, on, or after January 1, 1992. (b) This part does not apply to any property interest or power of appointment the validity of which has been determined in a judicial proceeding or by a settlement among interested persons."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21202 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, temporal and exclusionary scope of the statutory scheme (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21202.)

Each section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) and returned byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) both times. California's version is a modified adoption of the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities and may not be identical in every respect to the original Uniform Act or to another state's version of it; this clause describes only California's enacted text and does not independently compare it to the Uniform Act or to any other state's statute. Neither this clause nor the cited sections define "nonvested property interest"; no separate statutory definitions section for that term was located within Probate Code §§ 21200–21231, and the description of the term here reflects how the statute uses it rather than a quoted statutory definition. This is California-specific law; it does not describe the rule against perpetuities of any other state.

THE TWO-ALTERNATIVE VALIDITY TEST FOR A NONVESTED PROPERTY INTEREST
California's statutory Rule Against Perpetuities does not use a single test for whether a nonvested property interest is valid. Under Probate Code § 21205, a nonvested property interest is invalid unless it satisfies at least one of two separate alternatives. The first is the traditional alternative: when the interest is created, it is certain to vest or terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. The second is the independent 90-year "wait-and-see" alternative: the interest actually vests or terminates within 90 years after its creation, whether or not it was certain to do so when it was created. An interest that cannot satisfy the first alternative when created is not automatically invalid — it can still be validated later by actually vesting or terminating within the 90-year period, and an interest is likewise valid if it meets the first alternative even though the 90-year period would also have been satisfied. The statute treats these as two independent routes to validity, not as a single combined test, and an interest is invalid only if it fails both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A nonvested property interest is invalid unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) When the interest is created, it is certain to vest or terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. (b) The interest either vests or terminates within 90 years after its creation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21205 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the two-alternative statutory rule against perpetuities for a nonvested property interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21205.)

The section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) and returned byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) both times. California's version is a modified adoption of the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities and may not be identical in every respect to the original Uniform Act or to another state's version of it; no independent comparison to the Uniform Act or other states' statutes was performed. This clause does not address the parallel, separately codified rule for powers of appointment (Probate Code §§ 21206–21207) or the judicial reformation remedy (§ 21220), each addressed in other clauses of this document.

PARALLEL RULE FOR POWERS OF APPOINTMENT
California's statutory Rule Against Perpetuities applies its two-alternative validity structure not only to nonvested property interests but, separately, to powers of appointment. Probate Code § 21206 addresses a general power of appointment that is not presently exercisable because of a condition precedent: the power is invalid unless, when created, the condition precedent is certain to be satisfied or become impossible to satisfy no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive, or the condition precedent actually is satisfied or becomes impossible to satisfy within 90 years after the power's creation. Probate Code § 21207 applies the same two-alternative structure to a nongeneral power of appointment or a general testamentary power of appointment: the power is invalid unless, when created, it is certain to be irrevocably exercised or otherwise to terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive, or it actually is irrevocably exercised or otherwise terminates within 90 years after its creation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A general power of appointment not presently exercisable because of a condition precedent is invalid unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) When the power is created, the condition precedent is certain to be satisfied or become impossible to satisfy no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. (b) The condition precedent either is satisfied or becomes impossible to satisfy within 90 years after its creation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21206 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the two-alternative rule for a general power of appointment subject to a condition precedent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21206.)
  "A nongeneral power of appointment or a general testamentary power of appointment is invalid unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) When the power is created, it is certain to be irrevocably exercised or otherwise to terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. (b) The power is irrevocably exercised or otherwise terminates within 90 years after its creation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21207 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the two-alternative rule for a nongeneral power of appointment or a general testamentary power of appointment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21207.)
  Known gap: § 21206 and § 21207 are two separate California Probate Code sections, each independently fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) with byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times for each. They are independent code sections from each other and from § 21205 (the nonvested-property-interest rule addressed in a separate clause of this document), but all three sit within the same Article 2 of the same 1991 statutory scheme and apply the identical 21-years/90-years structure to different subject matter (a condition precedent to exercise, in § 21206, versus irrevocable exercise or termination, in § 21207) rather than confirming the same fact through independent means. This clause does not address every provision of Article 2 (§§ 21205–21209); a related provision, § 21231, separately addresses how an individual described only as the spouse of a living person is treated for purposes of measuring the 21-years-after-death alternative, and is not covered here.

JUDICIAL REFORMATION REMEDY FOR AN INTEREST THAT WOULD OTHERWISE VIOLATE THE RULE
California's statutory scheme provides a judicial reformation remedy rather than leaving every interest that would otherwise fail the rule permanently void. Under Probate Code § 21220, on the petition of an interested person, a court shall reform a disposition in the manner that most closely approximates the transferor's manifested plan of distribution, and the reformed disposition must itself stay within the 90 years allowed by the applicable provision in Article 2 (§§ 21205–21209). This remedy is available if any one of three conditions is satisfied: a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment has already become invalid under the statutory rule; a class gift is not yet invalid but might become invalid, and the time has arrived when the share of any class member is to take effect in possession or enjoyment; or a nonvested property interest that is not validated by the traditional 21-years-after-death alternative of § 21205(a) can vest, but not within 90 years after its creation. The reformation is framed as mandatory ("a court shall reform") once a petition is filed and one of the three triggering conditions is established, and it uses the transferor's own manifested plan of distribution — approximated as closely as possible within the 90-year outer limit — as its guiding standard, rather than simply voiding the interest or substituting a court's own preferred disposition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "On petition of an interested person, a court shall reform a disposition in the manner that most closely approximates the transferor’s manifested plan of distribution and is within the 90 years allowed by the applicable provision in Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205), if any of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) A nonvested property interest or a power of appointment becomes invalid under the statutory rule against perpetuities provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205). (b) A class gift is not but might become invalid under the statutory rule against perpetuities provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205), and the time has arrived when the share of any class member is to take effect in possession or enjoyment. (c) A nonvested property interest that is not validated by subdivision (a) of Section 21205 can vest but not within 90 years after its creation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21220 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the judicial reformation remedy for an interest that would otherwise violate the statutory rule against perpetuities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21220.)

Code § 21220, fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) with byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times. The section's own cross-references to § 21205 (repeated in the introductory clause and in subdivisions (a), (b), and (c)) are quotations of that same statutory language already addressed in this document's clause on the two-alternative test, not an independent source. § 21220 does not itself define "interested person" or specify the procedural mechanics of a reformation petition (for example, which court, what showing beyond the three listed conditions, or how competing petitions are resolved); this clause does not go beyond what § 21220 states to fill in those gaps. Whether a court will actually reform a given disposition, and what reformed terms it will adopt, depends on the specific facts and the transferor's actual manifested plan of distribution in each case — something this clause does not evaluate for any particular instrument.

STATUTORY EXCLUSIONS FROM THE RULE
The statutory rule of § 21205 does not apply to every nonvested property interest or power of appointment; Probate Code § 21225 lists categories the rule does not reach. Most broadly, the rule does not apply to a nonvested property interest or power of appointment arising out of a nondonative transfer — except that eight specifically listed categories of nondonative transfer remain subject to the rule despite arising from a bargained-for exchange rather than a gift: a premarital or postmarital agreement, a separation or divorce settlement, a spouse's election, a similar arrangement arising out of a marital relationship, a contract to make or not to revoke a will or trust, a contract to exercise or not to exercise a power of appointment, a transfer in satisfaction of a duty of support, or a reciprocal transfer. Separately excluded, without any carve-back, are: a fiduciary's power relating to the administration or management of assets, including the power to sell, lease, or mortgage property and the power to determine principal and income; a power to appoint a fiduciary; a trustee's discretionary power to distribute principal to a beneficiary who already holds an indefeasibly vested interest in the trust's income and principal, before the trust terminates; a nonvested property interest held by a charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision, where that interest is preceded by an interest held by another charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision; a nonvested property interest or power of appointment in a pension, profit-sharing, stock bonus, health, disability, death benefit, income deferral, or similar employee benefit plan, except one created by an election of a participant, beneficiary, or spouse; a property interest, power of appointment, or arrangement that was not subject to the common law rule against perpetuities or that is excluded by another California statute; and a trust created to provide benefits under hospital service contracts, group life insurance, group disability insurance, group annuities, or a combination of those, as defined in the Insurance Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205) does not apply to any of the following: (a) A nonvested property interest or a power of appointment arising out of a nondonative transfer, except a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment arising out of (1) a premarital or postmarital agreement, (2) a separation or divorce settlement, (3) a spouse’s election, (4) or a similar arrangement arising out of a prospective, existing, or previous marital relationship between the parties, (5) a contract to make or not to revoke a will or trust, (6) a contract to exercise or not to exercise a power of appointment, (7) a transfer in satisfaction of a duty of support, or (8) a reciprocal transfer. (b) A fiduciary’s power relating to the administration or management of assets, including the power of a fiduciary to sell, lease, or mortgage property, and the power of a fiduciary to determine principal and income. (c) A power to appoint a fiduciary. (d) A discretionary power of a trustee to distribute principal before termination of a trust to a beneficiary having an indefeasibly vested interest in the income and principal. (e) A nonvested property interest held by a charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision, if the nonvested property interest is preceded by an interest held by another charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision. (f) A nonvested property interest in or a power of appointment with respect to a trust or other property arrangement forming part of a pension, profit-sharing, stock bonus, health, disability, death benefit, income deferral, or other current or deferred benefit plan for one or more employees, independent contractors, or their beneficiaries or spouses, to which contributions are made for the purpose of distributing to or for the benefit of the participants or their beneficiaries or spouses the property, income, or principal in the trust or other property arrangement, except a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment that is created by an election of a participant or a beneficiary or spouse. (g) A property interest, power of appointment, or arrangement that was not subject to the common law rule against perpetuities or is excluded by another statute of this state. (h) A trust created for the purpose of providing for its beneficiaries under hospital service contracts, group life insurance, group disability insurance, group annuities, or any combination of such insurance, as defined in the Insurance Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21225 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, statutory exclusions from the rule against perpetuities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21225.)

Most broadly, the rule does not apply to a nonvested property interest or power of appointment arising out of a nondonative transfer — except that eight specifically listed categories of nondonative transfer remain subject to the rule despite arising from a bargained-for exchange rather than a gift: a premarital or postmarital agreement, a separation or divorce settlement, a spouse's election, a similar arrangement arising out of a marital relationship, a contract to make or not to revoke a will or trust, a contract to exercise or not to exercise a power of appointment, a transfer in satisfaction of a duty of support, or a reciprocal transfer. Separately excluded, without any carve-back, are: a fiduciary's power relating to the administration or management of assets, including the power to sell, lease, or mortgage property and the power to determine principal and income; a power to appoint a fiduciary; a trustee's discretionary power to distribute principal to a beneficiary who already holds an indefeasibly vested interest in the trust's income and principal, before the trust terminates; a nonvested property interest held by a charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision, where that interest is preceded by an interest held by another charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision; a nonvested property interest or power of appointment in a pension, profit-sharing, stock bonus, health, disability, death benefit, income deferral, or similar employee benefit plan, except one created by an election of a participant, beneficiary, or spouse; a property interest, power of appointment, or arrangement that was not subject to the common law rule against perpetuities or that is excluded by another California statute; and a trust created to provide benefits under hospital service contracts, group life insurance, group disability insurance, group annuities, or a combination of those, as defined in the Insurance Code.

citations.quote: Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205) does not apply to any of the following: (a) A nonvested property interest or a power of appointment arising out of a nondonative transfer, except a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment arising out of (1) a premarital or postmarital agreement, (2) a separation or divorce settlement, (3) a spouse’s election, (4) or a similar arrangement arising out of a prospective, existing, or previous marital relationship between the parties, (5) a contract to make or not to revoke a will or trust, (6) a contract to exercise or not to exercise a power of appointment, (7) a transfer in satisfaction of a duty of support, or (8) a reciprocal transfer. (b) A fiduciary’s power relating to the administration or management of assets, including the power of a fiduciary to sell, lease, or mortgage property, and the power of a fiduciary to determine principal and income. (c) A power to appoint a fiduciary. (d) A discretionary power of a trustee to distribute principal before termination of a trust to a beneficiary having an indefeasibly vested interest in the income and principal. (e) A nonvested property interest held by a charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision, if the nonvested property interest is preceded by an interest held by another charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision. (f) A nonvested property interest in or a power of appointment with respect to a trust or other property arrangement forming part of a pension, profit-sharing, stock bonus, health, disability, death benefit, income deferral, or other current or deferred benefit plan for one or more employees, independent contractors, or their beneficiaries or spouses, to which contributions are made for the purpose of distributing to or for the benefit of the participants or their beneficiaries or spouses the property, income, or principal in the trust or other property arrangement, except a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment that is created by an election of a participant or a beneficiary or spouse. (g) A property interest, power of appointment, or arrangement that was not subject to the common law rule against perpetuities or is excluded by another statute of this state. (h) A trust created for the purpose of providing for its beneficiaries under hospital service contracts, group life insurance, group disability insurance, group annuities, or any combination of such insurance, as defined in the Insurance Code.

Subdivision (a)'s structure is a double exclusion — the rule generally does not apply to nondonative transfers, but the eight listed categories are carved back out of that exclusion and so remain subject to the rule — and this clause's description preserves that structure rather than simplifying it into a single list. This clause does not independently verify how § 21225(f)'s cross-referenced federal or state employee-benefit-plan concepts (for example, what qualifies as a "pension" or "profit-sharing" plan for this purpose) are defined elsewhere; it states only what § 21225 itself says.
